display.h1: The Rule of Three in Writing: An Australian Writer's Guide to Making Your Words Memorable

body:
You've heard it a hundred times: "use the rule of three." But when you actually sit down to write, the advice goes vague fast. You end up bolting three near-identical adjectives onto a sentence like a shopping list, or forcing a triplet where one word would've done the job just fine.

Here's the thing: the rule of three isn't really a rule. It's a rhythm that's been running through Australian storytelling long before anyone put a label on it, from the pub yarn to Paul Keating's Redfern Address. Once you hear it, you start spotting it everywhere, and you can't quite unhear it again.

This guide walks through why three works, where it already lives in Australian writing you probably admire, and how to use it deliberately in your own fiction, business writing, persuasive essays, speeches, and blog posts, plus when to break the pattern for something even more effective.

By the end, you'll have a working toolkit rather than a slogan you nod along to and forget by Tuesday. Let's get into it.

After a decade spent editing manuscripts, pitch decks, and speeches for Australian writers, the pattern I notice first in any draft is still this one, sometimes it's there when it shouldn't be, more often it's missing when it should be doing the heavy lifting.

What Is the Rule of Three, Exactly?

If you've searched for the rule of three meaning or a plain rule of three definition, here it is in one line: it's the writing principle that ideas, phrases, or events presented in groups of three feel more satisfying and memorable than groups of two or four. Think "blood, sweat and tears," or "beginning, middle, end." Three is the smallest number that reads as a deliberate pattern rather than a coincidence, two just looks like a pair, four starts to feel like a list.

It's not a modern marketing trick, either. Oral storytelling cultures, including Indigenous Australian songlines and Greek myth, have long used triadic repetition to help stories travel and stick in memory without being written down. Classical orators leaned on the same instinct: Cicero's tricolon strung three parallel words or clauses together to build persuasive momentum, a technique modern speechwriters still borrow without necessarily knowing where it came from.

Why Three Works: A Bit of the Psychology

Your brain is a pattern-seeking machine, and three is the minimum number that actually forms a pattern. One item is just a point. Two is a comparison. Three is a shape, and shapes are what our brains latch onto and remember. That's also why triads are lighter to read than a longer list: "she arrived, she saw, she conquered" takes less cognitive effort to process than the same idea stretched across five clauses.

This echoes psychologist George Miller's well-known research into the limits of short-term memory, which found that our minds handle small chunks of information far more comfortably than large ones. Three sits neatly inside that comfort zone, which is probably part of why it feels so natural to both write and read. There's ongoing cognitive science interest in exactly how rhythmic language gets processed and recalled, if this is your kind of rabbit hole, it's worth digging into current research from Australian university psychology departments rather than taking any single figure as gospel.

In practice, this means the third item in a series is the one readers remember longest. Save your strongest point, image, or punchline for last, it's doing more memory work than the two that came before it.

The Rule of Three in Australian Writing and Speech

Some of the most quoted moments in Australian public life lean on this pattern hard. Paul Keating's 1992 Redfern Address is the standout example: he stacks short, blunt admissions one after another, the dispossession, the diseases and alcohol, the murders, the stolen children, and the power comes from accumulation rather than any single quotable line. Julia Gillard's 2012 misogyny speech works a similar trick with rhetorical questions, each one landing a beat harder than the last as she corners her opponent.

Australian fiction uses the same instinct. Tim Winton's Cloudstreet is often read as a triad in itself: the Pickles family, the Lambs, and the sprawling shared house that behaves almost like a third character. Liane Moriarty's Big Little Lies is built explicitly around three narrators, Madeline, Celeste and Jane, whose separate secrets fold into one shared reckoning by the end. And Banjo Paterson's "The Man from Snowy River" often falls into three-beat phrases that mirror the rhythm of a horse at full gallop.

Non-fiction does it too. Helen Garner's essays frequently move in three stages, what happened, what she made of it, and what it reveals, which is well worth studying if you write memoir or personal essays yourself.

You'll spot it in advertising as well. Carlton Draught's "Big Ad" campaign built its entire joke around one escalating idea repeated and inflated past the point of reason, a classic pattern-then-punchline structure Australian comedy leans on constantly. For nearly two decades, Bunnings' tagline was built around a similarly punchy, memorable shape before the brand retired it in 2020. Even news outlets reach for triads in headline writing, three linked events, three key numbers, because a pattern of three compresses a lot of context into something scannable in half a second.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander storytelling deserves its own mention here, and its own care. Oral traditions across the many distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures often use repetition and pattern to help carry law, history, and knowledge across generations, techniques that predate written rhetoric by tens of thousands of years. This is a brief, respectful gesture toward a much deeper subject than one paragraph can hold; if you want to understand these traditions properly, the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS) is the right place to start, and Indigenous-led resources will always tell that story better than a craft blog can.

Putting the Rule of Three to Work, Genre by Genre

Fiction. Even a short story benefits from a clear three-act shape: setup, development, resolution. Character trios work the same way, think Harry, Ron and Hermione, where each character carries a different piece of the protagonist's journey. And the "rule of three attempts" is a genuine craft tool: let your protagonist try and fail twice before succeeding on the third go. It's a simple way to earn an ending instead of rushing it. If you're mapping this out, it's worth reading up on how to outline a novel before you start drafting scenes, and on the mechanics of protagonist vs antagonist dynamics if your trio needs sharper tension. For shorter work, our guide on how to write a short story covers the same three-beat shape in miniature.

Non-fiction, memoir, and persuasive writing

The classic three-part essay, introduction, body, conclusion, still holds up because it keeps readers oriented. If you're structuring a persuasive essay in Australia for school, uni, or work, the shape barely changes: state your claim, back it with a small cluster of supporting points with the strongest saved for last, then close by telling the reader what you want them to think, feel, and do. Many Australian classrooms teach a close cousin of this called the OREO structure, opinion, reason, example, opinion, which bookends an argument so the opinion is the first and last thing a reader hears. For a persuasive essay introduction or a persuasive speech opening, simple starters like "consider this," "imagine if," or "the evidence is clear" all do the same job: they signal you're about to build a case, not just make a claim. Memoir works on a similar three-part emotional arc, the way things were, the moment of change, the way things are now.

Business writing 

The problem–solution–benefit triad persists because it mirrors how people actually decide things. Email structure follows the same logic in miniature: subject line as hook, opening line as context, call to action as the ask, three elements, no padding. Reports and proposals land better when findings are grouped into three key takeaways, since busy executives skim rather than read. Melbourne-based business storytelling expert Yamini Naidu makes a related point in her work with corporate leaders: dry facts and data fade quickly, but a story shaped around a clear pattern sticks, and grouping your key points in threes is one of the simplest ways to give a pitch that shape.

Speechwriting 

The tricolon crescendo is the classic move: build three phrases so the last one lands hardest. Churchill's wartime address is the textbook example, he repeats the same phrase across a widening list of places, each repetition landing with more weight than the one before. Repetition with variation works similarly: say the same line three times, adding a new layer of meaning each time. Close with a three-part call to action: what you want your audience to think, feel, and do.

Content marketing and digital writing 

Headlines like "3 Ways to..." or "The Only 3 Tools You Need" promise something digestible and specific in a way "several ways" never quite manages. Listicles read better in groups of three per section rather than as one long undifferentiated dump. Australian brands like Canva and Who Gives A Crap use this instinct constantly in their blog headlines, worth keeping a swipe file of the ones that catch your eye.

Common Mistakes (and When Two or Four Beats Three)

The most common failure is the lazy triplet, three adjectives that all mean roughly the same thing, like "big, large, huge." That's bulk, not meaning. Each item in a triad needs to earn its place by adding something the others don't.

The second failure is overuse. If every paragraph contains a triad, the pattern stops feeling deliberate and starts feeling like a tic. Vary your sentence structure so the technique stays a technique rather than becoming white noise.

And sometimes three is simply the wrong number. A pair can feel complete on its own, "love and loss" doesn't need a third element to round it out, and adding one would probably dilute it. In technical or safety writing, clarity beats rhythm outright: "Danger: high voltage" doesn't want a poetic third beat, it wants to be understood in half a second.

There's also a subversive use worth knowing. Australian comedians like Hannah Gadsby and Shaun Micallef regularly set up a triad only to break it for a laugh, the first two items establish the pattern, and the third undercuts it entirely. This works because readers have been trained, consciously or not, to expect the third beat to complete rather than contradict. That's exactly why it lands as a joke instead of a typo. If you want to see how expectation gets subverted more broadly in fiction, our piece on types of irony in Australian literature is a useful next read.

Quick Exercises to Train Your Ear

  • Spot the triad. Grab a recent Miles Franklin winner or a copy of The Monthly and highlight every instance of the rule of three you can find, whether it's in a single sentence or the shape of a whole chapter.

  • Rewrite a famous speech. Take a section of Keating's Redfern Address or Gillard's misogyny speech and restructure it, turn a pair into a triad, or break a long triad into a pair plus a standalone line. Read both versions aloud and notice what changes.

  • Three-sentence story. Write a complete story in exactly three sentences, setup, conflict, resolution, set somewhere distinctly Australian: a beach Christmas, a footy grand final, a drought-breaking storm.

Self-audit checklist, for your next editing pass:

  • Do any of your triads contain near-synonyms that could be swapped for something more distinct?

  • Is the third element genuinely the strongest, or does the order need reshuffling?

  • Have you used the rule of three more than twice in one section? If so, vary at least one instance.

  • Is each triad doing real work for the reader, or is it decorative? Cut it if it's decorative.

  • In fiction, does your protagonist attempt something three times, or could a third attempt raise the stakes?

  • Have you read the piece aloud to check whether the rhythm actually lands?

Tools Worth Knowing

A few resources make this easier to practise rather than just understand. Scrivener's corkboard view is genuinely handy for visually mapping a three-act structure or a three-part essay. ProWritingAid's repetition report is useful for catching both the lazy triplet and pattern overuse in a finished draft. The Australian Writers' Centre and Writing NSW both run courses that touch on rhetorical technique with a local slant. And Kate Forsyth, who teaches the rule of three in her own workshops, puts it simply on her writing journal: humans are pattern-loving creatures, and that's really the whole idea in one sentence.

If you'd rather have a professional pair of eyes on your manuscript's rhythm than chase it alone, our professional editing service is built for exactly this kind of pass. And if you're further back in the process and want someone else to shape the story first, our fiction ghostwriting and non-fiction ghostwriting teams build these patterns in from the first draft.

Further Reading

For deeper craft study, the Australian Writers' Centre and Writing NSW both offer workshops led by published authors. AIATSIS remains the most authoritative starting point for readers wanting to properly understand Indigenous Australian storytelling traditions, well beyond what a single blog section can cover.

faqs.q: What is the rule of three in writing?
faqs.a: It's the idea that ideas, phrases, or events grouped in threes feel more complete and memorable than groups of two or four. Three is the smallest number that reads as a genuine pattern rather than a coincidence.

faqs.q: What's a good rule of three example?
faqs.a: Classic ones include "blood, sweat and tears" and "beginning, middle, end." In Australian speechwriting, Paul Keating's Redfern Address is a widely studied example of the technique used at length.

faqs.q: How do I structure a persuasive essay in Australia?
faqs.a: Most Australian curricula teach a three-part shape: state your claim, support it with evidence (often using the OREO scaffold, opinion, reason, example, opinion), then restate what you want the reader to think, feel, or do.

faqs.q: How should I start a persuasive essay or speech?
faqs.a: Open with something that earns attention rather than a flat thesis statement, a short scenario, a pointed question, or a bold claim you'll go on to prove. Save the formal thesis for the sentence right after the hook.

faqs.q: What is the OREO writing structure?
faqs.a: It stands for opinion, reason, example, opinion. It's taught widely in Australian schools as a scaffold for persuasive paragraphs, and it works for a similar reason the rule of three does, it gives an argument a clear, repeatable shape.

faqs.q: Is two or four ever better than three?
faqs.a: Yes. A pair can feel complete without a third element, "love and loss" is a good example, and technical or safety writing usually wants clarity over rhythm, so a fourth point should be included if it's genuinely needed rather than dropped to force a triad.

faqs.q: How do I practise the rule of three without sounding formulaic?
faqs.a: Vary how often you use it, make sure every element in a triad adds something distinct, and read your work aloud. If a triad feels forced when spoken, it usually is.

faqs.q: Does the rule of three work in business writing and pitches?
faqs.a: Yes, the problem-solution-benefit structure is one of the most common triads in business communication, and grouping report findings or email points into three tends to make them easier for busy readers to retain.

faqs.q: Where can Australian writers learn more about the rule of three?
faqs.a: The Australian Writers' Centre, Writing NSW, and Kate Forsyth's own writing journal are all solid starting points, alongside any recent Miles Franklin-winning novel if you want to see the pattern working in the wild.

faqs.q: Does the rule of three apply to fiction and non-fiction equally?
faqs.a: Yes, though it shows up differently, three-act structure and character trios in fiction, three-part arguments and essay structures in non-fiction, and repetition-with-variation in speeches.
